entries.5d36c6bd8253a21ea1eeb3ac944603c7e0b61ca9: <div sID="gen5858" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="27" osisID="1Sam.27" sID="1Sam.27"/> <div eID="gen5858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5859" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5860" type="x-p"/> David was a man after God's own heart, and yet he had his faults, which are recorded, not for our imitation, but for our admonition; witness the story of this chapter, in which, though, I. We find, to his praise, that he prudently took care of his own safety and his family's (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.2-1Sam.27.4">ver. 2-4</reference>) and valiantly fought Israel's battles against the Canaanites (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.8-1Sam.27.9">ver. 8-9</reference>), yet, II. We find, to his dishonour, 1. That he began to despair of his deliverance, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1">ver. 1</reference>. 2. That he deserted his own country, and went to dwell in the land of the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.5-1Sam.27.7">5-7</reference>. 3. That he imposed upon Achish with an equivocation, if not a lie, concerning his expedition, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.10-1Sam.27.12">ver. 10-12</reference>.
entries.70d29f52a7023f4507faddc91f640d49ba424f4a: <div eID="gen5860" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5859" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David Returns to Gath. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1055.)</title> <div sID="gen5861" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And David said in his heart, I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> nothing better for me than that I should speedily escape into the land of the Philistines; and Saul shall despair of me, to seek me any more in any coast of Israel: so shall I escape out of his hand. <hi type="super">2</hi> And David arose, and he passed over with the six hundred men that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him unto Achish, the son of Maoch, king of Gath. <hi type="super">3</hi> And David dwelt with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, <hi type="italic">even</hi> David with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and Abigail the Carmelitess, Nabal's wife. <hi type="super">4</hi> And it was told Saul that David was fled to Gath: and he sought no more again for him. <hi type="super">5</hi> And David said unto Achish, If I have now found grace in thine eyes, let them give me a place in some town in the country, that I may dwell there: for why should thy servant dwell in the royal city with thee? <hi type="super">6</hi> Then Achish gave him Ziklag that day: wherefore Ziklag pertaineth unto the kings of Judah unto this day. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the time that David dwelt in the country of the Philistines was a full year and four months. <div eID="gen5861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5862" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The prevalency of David's fear, which was the effect of the weakness of his faith (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">He said to his heart</hi> (so it may be read), in his communings with it concerning his present condition, <hi type="italic">I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul.</hi> He represented to himself the restless rage and malice of Saul (who could not be wrought into a reconciliation) and the treachery of his own countrymen, witness that of the Ziphites, once and again; he looked upon his own forces, and observed how few they were, and that no recruits had come in to him for a great while, nor could he perceive that he got any ground; and hence, in a melancholy mood, he draws this dark conclusion: <hi type="italic">I shall one day perish by the hand of Saul.</hi> But, <hi type="italic">O thou of little faith! wherefore dost thou doubt?</hi> Was he not anointed to be king? Did not that imply an assurance that he should be preserved to the kingdom? Though he had no reason to trust Saul's promises, had he not all the reason in the world to trust the promises of God? His experience of the particular care Providence took of him ought to have encouraged him. He that has delivered does and will. But unbelief is a sin that easily besets even good men. When <hi type="italic">without are fightings, within are fears,</hi> and it is a hard matter to get over them. <hi type="italic">Lord, increase our faith!</hi> <div eID="gen5862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5863" type="x-p"/> II. The resolution he came to hereupon. Now that Saul had, for this time, returned to his place, he determined to take this opportunity of retiring into the Philistines' country. Consulting his own heart only, and not the ephod or the prophet, he concludes, <hi type="italic">There is nothing better for me than that I should speedily escape into the land of the Philistines.</hi> Long trials are in danger of tiring the faith and patience even of very good men. Now, 1. Saul was an enemy to himself and his kingdom in driving David to this extremity. He weakened his own interest when he expelled from his service, and forced into the service of his enemies, so great a general as David was, and so brave a regiment as he had the command of. 2. David was no friend to himself in taking this course. God had appointed him to set up his standard <hi type="italic">in the land of Judah,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.5">ch. xxii. 5</reference>. There God had wonderfully preserved him, and employed him sometimes for the good of his country; why then should he think of deserting his post? How could he expect the protection of the God of Israel if he went out of the borders of the land of Israel? Could he expect to be safe among the Philistines, out of whose hands he had lately escaped so narrowly by feigning himself mad? Would he receive obligations from those now whom he knew he must not return kindness to when he should come to be king, but be under an obligation to make war upon? Hereby he would gratify his enemies, who bade him go and serve other gods that they might have wherewith to reproach him, and very much weaken the hands of his friends, who would not have wherewith to answer that reproach. See what need we have to pray, <hi type="italic">Lord, lead us not into temptation.</hi> <div eID="gen5863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5864" type="x-p"/> III. The kind reception he had at Gath. Achish bade him welcome, partly out of generosity, being proud of entertaining so brave a man, partly out of policy, hoping to engage him for ever to his service, and that his example would invite many more to desert and come over to him. No doubt he gave David a solemn promise of protection, which he could rely upon when he could not trust Saul's promises. We may blush to think that the word of a Philistine should go further than the word of an Israelite, who, if an Israelite indeed, would be without guile, and that the city of Gath should be a place of refuge for a good man when the cities of Israel refuse him a safe abode. David, 1. Brought his men with him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.2">v. 2</reference>) that they might guard him, and might themselves be safe where he was, and to recommend himself the more to Achish, who hoped to have service out of him. 2. He brought his family with him, his <hi type="italic">wives</hi> and <hi type="italic">his household,</hi> so did all <hi type="italic">his men,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.2-1Sam.27.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. Masters of families ought to take care of those that are committed to them, to protect and provide for those of their own house, and to <hi type="italic">dwell with them as men of knowledge.</hi> <div eID="gen5864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5865" type="x-p"/> IV. Saul's desisting from the further prosecution of him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">He sought no more again for him;</hi> this intimates that notwithstanding the professions of repentance he had lately made, if he had had David in his reach, he would have aimed another blow. But, because he dares not come where he is, he resolves to let him alone. Thus many seem to leave their sins, but really their sins leave them; they would persist in them if they could. Saul sought no more for him, contenting himself with his banishment, since he could not have his blood, and hoping, it may be (as he had done, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.25">ch. xviii. 25</reference>), that he would, some time or other, <hi type="italic">fall by the hand of the Philistines;</hi> and, though he would rather have the pleasure of destroying him himself, yet, if they do it, he will be satisfied, so that it be done effectually. <div eID="gen5865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5866" type="x-p"/> V. David's removal from Gath to Ziklag. <div eID="gen5866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5867" type="x-p"/> 1. David's request for leave to remove was prudent and very modest, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.5">v. 5</reference>. (1.) It was really prudent. David knew what it was to be envied in the court of Saul, and had much more reason to fear in the court of Achish, and therefore declines preferment there, and wishes for a settlement in the country, where he might be private, more within himself, and less in other people's way. In a town of his own he might have the more free exercise of his religion, and keep his men better to it, and not have his righteous soul vexed, as it was at Gath, with the idolatries of the Philistines. (2.) As it was presented to Achish it was very modest. He does not prescribe to him what place he should assign him, only begs it may be in some town in the country, where he pleased (beggars must not be choosers); but he gives this for a reason, "<hi type="italic">Why should thy servant dwell in the royal city,</hi> to crowd thee, and disoblige those about thee?" Note, Those that would stand fast must not covet to stand high; and humble souls aim not to dwell in royal cities. <div eID="gen5867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5868" type="x-p"/> 2. The grant which Achish made to him, upon that request, was very generous and kind (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.6-1Sam.27.7">v. 6, 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Achish gave him Ziklag.</hi> Hereby, (1.) Israel recovered their ancient right; for Ziklag was in the lot of the tribe of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.31">Josh. xv. 31</reference>), and afterwards, out of that lot, was assigned, with some other cities, to Simeon, <reference osisRef="Josh.19.5">Josh. xix. 5</reference>. But either it was never subdued, or the Philistines had, in some struggle with Israel, made themselves masters of it. Perhaps they had got it unjustly, and Achish, being a man of sense and honour, took this occasion to restore it. <hi type="italic">The righteous God judgeth righteously.</hi> (2.) David gained a commodious settlement, not only at a distance from Gath, but bordering upon Israel, where he might keep up a correspondence with his own countrymen, and whither they might resort to him at the revolution that was now approaching. Though we do not find that he augmented his forces at all while Saul lived (for, <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.10">ch. xxx. 10</reference>, he had but his <hi type="italic">six hundred men</hi>), yet, immediately after Saul's death, that was the rendezvous of his friends. Nay, it should seem, while he kept himself close because of Saul, multitudes resorted to him, at least to assure him of their sincere intentions, <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.1-1Chr.12.22">1 Chron. xii. 1-22</reference>. And this further advantage David gained, that Ziklag was annexed to the crown, at least the royalty of it pertained to the kings of Judah, ever after, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.6">v. 6</reference>. Note, There is nothing lost by humility and modesty, and a willingness to retire. Real advantages follow those that flee from imaginary honours. Here David continued for some days, even <hi type="italic">four months,</hi> as it may very well be read (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.7">v. 7</reference>), or some days above four months: the LXX. reads it, <hi type="italic">some months;</hi> so long he waited for the set time of his accession to the throne; for <hi type="italic">he that believeth shall not make haste.</hi>
entries.93656dad76e5b770f31f377dd7eafed6e609fa5a: <div eID="gen5868" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Smites the Amalekites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1055.)</title> <div sID="gen5869" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> And David and his men went up, and invaded the Geshurites, and the Gezrites, and the Amalekites: for those <hi type="italic">nations were</hi> of old the inhabitants of the land, as thou goest to Shur, even unto the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">9</hi> And David smote the land, and left neither man nor woman alive, and took away the sheep, and the oxen, and the asses, and the camels, and the apparel, and returned, and came to Achish. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Achish said, Whither have ye made a road to day? And David said, Against the south of Judah, and against the south of the Jerahmeelites, and against the south of the Kenites. <hi type="super">11</hi> And David saved neither man nor woman alive, to bring <hi type="italic">tidings</hi> to Gath, saying, Lest they should tell on us, saying, So did David, and so <hi type="italic">will be</hi> his manner all the while he dwelleth in the country of the Philistines. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Achish believed David, saying, He hath made his people Israel utterly to abhor him; therefore he shall be my servant for ever. <div eID="gen5869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5870" type="x-p"/> Here is an account of David's actions while he was in the land of the Philistines, a fierce attack he made upon some remains of the devoted nations, his success in it, and the representation he gave of it to Achish. 1. We may acquit him of injustice and cruelty in this action because those people whom he cut off were such as heaven had long since doomed to destruction, and he that did it was one whom heaven had ordained to dominion; so that the thing was very fit to be done, and he was very fit to do it. It was not for him that was anointed to fight the Lord's battles to sit still in sloth, however he might think fit, in modesty, to retire. He desired to be safe from Saul only that he might expose himself for Israel. He avenged an old quarrel that God had with these nations, and at the same time fetched in provisions for himself and his army, for by their swords they must live. The Amalekites were to be all cut off. Probably the Geshurites and Gezrites were branches of Amalek. Saul was rejected for sparing them, David makes up the deficiency of his obedience before he succeeds him. He smote them, and <hi type="italic">left none alive,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.8-1Sam.27.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. The service paid itself, for they carried off abundance of spoil, which served for the subsistence of David's forces. 2. Yet we cannot acquit him of dissimulation with Achish in the account he gave him of this expedition. (1.) David, it seems, was not willing that he should know the truth, and therefore spared none to carry tidings to Gath (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.11">v. 11</reference>), not because he was ashamed of what he had done as a bad thing, but because he was afraid, if the Philistines knew it, they would be apprehensive of danger to themselves or their allies by harbouring him among them and would expel him from their coasts. It would be easy to conclude, <hi type="italic">If so he did, so will be his manner,</hi> and therefore he industriously conceals it from them, which, it seems, he could do by putting them all to the sword, for none of their neighbours would inform against him, nor perhaps would soon come to the knowledge of what was done, intelligence not being so readily communicated then as now. (2.) He hid it from Achish with an equivocation not at all becoming his character. Being asked which way he had made his sally, he answered, <hi type="italic">Against the south of Judah,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.13">v. 13</reference>. It was true he had invaded those countries that lay south of Judah, but he made Achish believe he had invaded those that lay south in Judah, the Ziphites for example, that had once and again betrayed him; so Achish understood him, and thence inferred that he <hi type="italic">had made his people Israel to abhor him,</hi> and so riveted himself in the interest of Achish. The fidelity of Achish to him, his good opinion of him, and the confidence he put in him, aggravate his sin in deceiving him thus, which, with some other such instances, David seems penitently to reflect upon when he prays, <hi type="italic">Remove from me the way of lying.</hi>  <chapter eID="1Sam.27"/> <div eID="gen5870" type="x-p"/>

entries.e5d93ed05d9f84c5c0c02fc4f484419c32d4685f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2787"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 27</title> <div sID="gen3817" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1-1Sam.27.4">1Sa 27:1-4</reference>. Saul Hearing That David Was Fled to Gath, Seeks No More for Him.<div eID="gen3817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3818" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2787"/><hi type="bold">1. David said in his heart, ... there is nothing better for me than that I should speedily escape into the land of the Philistines--</hi>This resolution of David's was, in every respect, wrong: (1) It was removing him from the place where the divine oracle intimated him to remain (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.5">1Sa 22:5</reference>); (2) It was rushing into the idolatrous land, for driving him into which he had denounced an imprecation on his enemies (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.19">1Sa 26:19</reference>); (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.3">3</reference>) It was a withdrawal of his counsel and aid from God's people. It was a movement, however, overruled by Providence to detach him from his country and to let the disasters impending over Saul and his followers be brought on by the Philistines. <div eID="gen3818" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1fa591d3655a326405c0196428527bad9bbb68f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2788"/><div sID="gen3819" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2788"/><hi type="bold">2-3. Achish, the son of Maoch, king of Gath--</hi>The popular description of this king's family creates a presumption that he was a different king from the reigning sovereign on David's first visit to Gath. Whether David had received a special invitation from him or a mere permission to enter his territories, cannot be determined. It is probable that the former was the case. From the universal notoriety given to the feud between Saul and David, which had now become irreconcilable, it might appear to Achish good policy to harbor him as a guest, and so the better pave the way for the hostile measures against Israel which the Philistines were at this time meditating.<div eID="gen3819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3820" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.5-1Sam.27.12">1Sa 27:5-12</reference>. David Begs Ziklag of Achish. <div eID="gen3820" type="x-p"/>
entries.1805b12826abc69f2fd360fef0ebf91e08ba630a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2789"/><div sID="gen3821" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2789"/><hi type="bold">5. let them give me a place in some town in the country--</hi>It was a prudent arrangement on the part of David; for it would prevent him being an object of jealous suspicion, or of mischievous plots among the Philistines. It would place his followers more beyond the risk of contamination by the idolatries of the court and capital; and it would give him an opportunity of making reprisals on the freebooting tribes that infested the common border of Israel and the Philistines. <div eID="gen3821" type="x-p"/>
entries.f09df53b6b2a347388b318f3b438b182fcf9d952: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2790"/><div sID="gen3822" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2790"/><hi type="bold">6. Ziklag--</hi>Though originally assigned to Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.31">Jos 15:31</reference>), and subsequently to Simeon (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.5">Jos 19:5</reference>), this town had never been possessed by the Israelites. It belonged to the Philistines, who gave it to David. <div eID="gen3822" type="x-p"/>
entries.31037f0b2315c19015f035833a0d1e78e5e60814: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2791"/><div sID="gen3823" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2791"/><hi type="bold">8. David ... went up, and invaded the Geshurites--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="Josh.13.2">Jos 13:2</reference>).<div eID="gen3823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3824" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the Gezrites--</hi>or the Gerizi [Gesenius], (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.12">Jos 12:12</reference>), some Arab horde which had once encamped there.<div eID="gen3824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the Amalekites--</hi>Part of the district occupied by them lay on the south of the land of Israel (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.14">Jud 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.12.15">12:15</reference>). <div eID="gen3825" type="x-p"/>
entries.52b75f52fd655d092c064b6804fa2079574badba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2792"/><div sID="gen3826" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2792"/><hi type="bold">10. Achish said, Whither have ye made a road to-day?--</hi>that is, raid, a hostile excursion for seizing cattle and other booty.<div eID="gen3826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3827" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">David said, Against the south of Judah, and against the south of the Jerahmeelites--</hi>Jerahmeel was the great-grandson of Judah, and his posterity occupied the southern portion of that tribal domain.<div eID="gen3827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the south of the Kenites--</hi>the posterity of Jethro, who occupied the south of Judah (<reference osisRef="Judg.1.16">Jud 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.24.21">Nu 24:21</reference>). The deceit practised upon his royal host and the indiscriminate slaughter committed, lest any one should escape to tell the tale, exhibit an unfavorable view of this part of David's history. <chapter eID="1Sam.27"/>

entries.efeb98713890a6b77f5d08fb9489c61eee5e4a1e: <div eID="gen10480" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10481" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10482" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10482" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10481" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10483" type="x-p"/> David flies to Achish, king of Gath, who receives him kindly, and gives him Ziklag to dwell in, where he continues a year and four months, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1-1Sam.27.7">1Sam 27:1-7</reference>. David invades the Geshurites and Amalekites, and leaves neither man nor woman alive, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.8">1Sam 27:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.9">1Sam 27:9</reference>. He returns to Achish, and pretends that he had been making inroads on the Israelites, and Achish believes it, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.10-1Sam.27.12">1Sam 27:10-12</reference>. <div eID="gen10483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10484" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10485" type="x-p"/> I shall now perish one day by the hand of Saul - This was a very hasty conclusion: God had so often interposed in behalf of his life, that he was authorized to believe the reverse. God had hitherto confounded all Saul's stratagems, and it was not at all likely that he would now abandon him: there was now no additional reason why he should withdraw from David his helping hand.
entries.928f519754406d81698d066e0bcad9c6cdab9323: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10486" type="x-p"/> David arose, and he passed over - unto Achish - There is not one circumstance in this transaction that is not blameable. David joins the enemies of his God and of his country, acts a most inhuman part against the Geshurites and Amalekites, without even the pretense of a Divine authority; tells a most deliberate falsehood to Achish, his protector, relative to the people against whom he had perpetrated this cruel act; giving him to understand that he had been destroying the Israelites, his enemies. I undertake no defense of this conduct of David; it is all bad, all defenceless; God vindicates him not. The inspired penman tells what he did, but passes no eulogium upon his conduct; and it is false to say that, because these things are recorded, therefore they are approved. In all these transactions David was in no sense a man after God's own heart. Chandler attempts to vindicate all this conduct: those who can receive his saying, let them receive it.
entries.8167734b8a3542d915b61bc9fe0551c465f44a86: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10487" type="x-p"/> Every man with his household - So it appears that the men who consorted with David had wives and families. David and his company resembled a tribe of the wandering Arabs.
entries.dda72cf7eb5b7232ee6ab738da5ee70d666a1f80: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen10487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10488" type="x-p"/> Why should thy servant dwell in the royal city - He seemed to intimate that two princely establishments in the same city were too many. Achish appears to have felt the propriety of his proposal, and therefore appoints him Ziklag.
entries.8762741dcae054fb57dc904a2bd77ed8c53d5a49: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10489" type="x-p"/> Achish gave him Ziklag - Ziklag was at first given to the tribe of Judah, but afterwards it was ceded to that of Simeon, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.31">Jos 15:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jos.19.5">Jos 19:5</reference>. The Philistines had, however, made themselves masters of it, and held it to the time here mentioned; it then fell into the tribe of Judah again, and continued to be the property of the kings of Judah. This verse is a proof that this book was written long after the days of Samuel, and that it was formed by a later hand, out of materials which had been collected by a contemporary author. See the preface.
entries.c521d7b97f31bb728a6de589fd45f81d2f42ce5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen10489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10490" type="x-p"/> David smote the land - Here was a complete extirpation of all these people, not one being left alive, lest he should carry tidings of the disasters of his country! The spoil which David took consisted of sheep, oxen, asses, camels, and apparel.
entries.731e8a71f4afca7b97fc7ce8e1322eaf9a5fa579: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen10490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10491" type="x-p"/> Whither have ye made a road today? - He had probably been in the habit of making predatory excursions. This seems to be implied in the question of Achish.
entries.74862c1e24274b11ca8246f2aea373c959a0afb4: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen10491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10492" type="x-p"/> He hath made his people - utterly to abhor him - This deception, which Dr. Delaney says "did harm to nobody, and to the account of which he is at an utter loss what degree of guilt to charge," imposed upon Achish, had the most direct tendency to make him imagine himself secure, while in the utmost danger; and to have a faithful friend and able ally in David, while he was the veriest enemy he could possibly have. Shame on him who becomes the apologist of such conduct! As to Dr. Chandler, he should know that no lie is of the truth, and that all falsity is an abomination to the Lord.  <chapter eID="1Sam.27"/> <div eID="gen10492" type="x-p"/>

entries.9291740b03151579cee84a56a42889e95d5993f8: <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1">1Sa 27:1</reference> <div eID="gen4141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4142" type="x-p"/> The result of the last affair with Saul, after his life had again been spared, could not fail to confirm David in his conviction that Saul would not desist from pursuing him, and that if he stayed any longer in the land, he would fall eventually into the hands of his enemy. With this conviction, he formed the following resolution: “<hi type="italic">Now shall I be consumed one day by the hand of Saul: there is no good to me</hi> (i.e., it will not be well with me if I remain in the land), <hi type="italic">but</hi> (כּי after a negative) <hi type="italic">I will flee into the land of the Philistines; so will Saul desist from me to seek me further</hi> (i.e., give up seeking me) <hi type="italic">in the whole of the territory of Israel, and I shall escape his hand</hi>.”
entries.20a955a1ae27dd5debf865236858353cef788ce0: <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.2">1Sa 27:2</reference> <div eID="gen4142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4143" type="x-p"/> Accordingly he went over with the 600 men who were with him to Achish, the king of Gath. <hi type="italic">Achish</hi>, the son of <hi type="italic">Maoch</hi>, is in all probability the same person not only as the king <hi type="italic">Achish</hi> mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.11">1Sa 21:11</reference>, but also as <hi type="italic">Achish</hi> the son of <hi type="italic">Maachah</hi> (1Ki 2:39), since <hi type="italic">Maoch</hi> and <hi type="italic">Maachah</hi> are certainly only different forms of the same name; and a fifty years’ reign, which we should have in that case to ascribe to Achish, it not impossible.
entries.0908b44223a1d1ce1bac963cdb12959ac4936192: <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.3-1Sam.27.4">1Sa 27:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen4143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4144" type="x-p"/> Achish allotted dwelling-places in his capital, Gath, for David and his wives, and for all his retinue; and Saul desisted from any further pursuit of David when he was informed of his flight to Gath. The <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> יוסף is apparently only a copyist’s error for יסף.
entries.0d84c35e29e470169175a0bca4f0d207dcba326d: <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.5-1Sam.27.6">1Sa 27:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen4144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4145" type="x-p"/> In the capital of the kingdom, however, David felt cramped, and therefore entreated Achish to assign him one of the land (or provincial) towns to dwell in; whereupon he gave him <hi type="italic">Ziklag</hi> for that purpose. This town was given to the Simeonites in the time of Joshua (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.5">Jos 19:5</reference>), but was afterwards taken by the Philistines, probably not long before the time of David, and appears to have been left without inhabitants in consequence of this conquest. The exact situation, in the western part of the Negeb, has not been clearly ascertained (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.31">Jos 15:31</reference>). Achish appears to have given it to David. This is implied in the remark, “<hi type="italic">Therefore Ziklag came to the kings of Judah</hi> (i.e., became their property) <hi type="italic">unto this day</hi>.”
entries.45509cc9656c1a8edfccd8e140d99b2e3022b364: <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.7">1Sa 27:7</reference> <div eID="gen4145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4146" type="x-p"/> The statement that David remained a year and four months in the land of the Philistines, is a proof of the historical character of the whole narrative. The ימים before the “four months” signifies <hi type="italic">a year</hi>; strictly speaking, a term of days which amounted to a full year (as in <reference osisRef="Lev.25.29">Lev 25:29</reference> : see also <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.3">1Sa 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.20">1Sa 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.19">1Sa 2:19</reference>).
entries.329763d13415b108e24cc3f9c62ab813dff23a1a: <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.8-1Sam.27.9">1Sa 27:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen4146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4147" type="x-p"/> From Ziklag David made an attack upon the Geshurites, Gerzites, and Amalekites, smote them without leaving a man alive, and returned with much booty. The occasion of this attack is not mentioned, as being a matter of indifference in relation to the chief object of the history; but it is no doubt to be sought for in plundering incursions made by these tribes into the land of Israel. For David would hardly have entered upon such a war in the situation in which he was placed at that time without some such occasion, seeing that it would be almost sure to bring him into suspicion with Achish, and endanger his safety. ויּעל, “<hi type="italic">he advanced</hi>,” the verb being used, as it frequently is, to denote the advance of an army against a people or town (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.8.1">Jos 8:1</reference>). At the same time, the tribes which he attacked may have had their seat upon the mountain plateau in the northern portion of the desert of Paran, so that David was obliged to march <hi type="italic">up</hi> to reach them. פּשׁט, <hi type="italic">to invade</hi> for the purpose of devastation and plunder. <hi type="italic">Geshuri</hi> is a tribe mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.13.2">Jos 13:2</reference> as living in the south of the territory of the Philistines, and is a different tribe from the Geshurites in the north-east of Gilead (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.5">Jos 12:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.11">Jos 13:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.13">Jos 13:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.3.14">Deu 3:14</reference>). These are the only passages in which they are mentioned. The <hi type="italic">Gerzites</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Gizrites</hi> according to the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>, are entirely unknown. Bonfrere and Clericus suppose them to be the <hi type="italic">Gerreni</hi> spoken of in 2 Macc. 13:24, who inhabited the town of <hi type="italic">Gerra</hi>, between Rhinocolura and Pelusium (Strabo, xvi. 760), or <hi type="italic">Gerron</hi> (Ptol. iv. 5). This conjecture is a possible one, but is very uncertain nevertheless, as the Gerzites certainly dwelt somewhere in the desert of Arabia. At any rate <hi type="italic">Grotius</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> cannot be correct in their opinion that they were the inhabitants of <hi type="italic">Gezer</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.33">Jos 10:33</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Amalekites</hi> were the remnant of this old hereditary foe of the Israelites, who had taken to flight on Saul’s war of extermination, and had now assembled again (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.8-1Sam.15.9">1Sa 15:8-9</reference>). “<hi type="italic">For they inhabit the land, where you go from of old to Shur, even to the land of Egypt</hi>.” The עשׁר before מעולם may be explained from the fact that בּואך is not adverbial here, but is construed according to its form as an infinitive: literally, “<hi type="italic">where from of old thy coming is to Shur</hi>.” עשׁר cannot have crept into the text through a copyist’s mistake, as such a mistake would not have found its way into all the MSS. The fact that the early translators did not render the word proves nothing against its genuineness, but merely shows that the translators regarded it as superfluous. Moreover, the Alexandrian text is decidedly faulty here, and עולם is confounded with עלם, ἀπὸ Γελάμ. <hi type="italic">Shur</hi> is the desert of <hi type="italic">Jifar</hi>, which is situated in front of Egypt (as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.7">1Sa 15:7</reference>). These tribes were nomads, and had large flocks, which David took with him as booty when he had smitten the tribes themselves. After his return, David betook himself to Achish, to report to the Philistian king concerning his enterprise, and deceive him as to its true character.
entries.0744aed33e6c6910b5acd61832db3a7f5ff46542: <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.10-1Sam.27.11">1Sa 27:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen4147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4148" type="x-p"/> Achish said, “<hi type="italic">Ye have not made an invasion to-day, have ye?</hi>” אל, like μὴ, is an interrogative sense; the ה has dropped out: vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §324, b. David replied, “Against the south of Judah, and the south of the Jerahmeelites, and into the south of the Kenites,” sc., we have made an incursion. This reply shows that the Geshurites, Gerzites, and Amalekites dwelt close to the southern boundary of Judah, so that David was able to represent the march against these tribes to Achish as a march against the south of Judah, to make him believe that he had been making an attack upon the southern territory of Judah and its dependencies. The Negeb of Judah is the land between the mountains of Judah and the desert of Arabia (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.21">Jos 15:21</reference>). The Jerahmeelites are the descendants of Jerahmeel, the first-born of Hezron (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.9">1Ch 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.25-1Chr.2.26">1Ch 2:25-26</reference>), and therefore one of the three large families of Judah who sprang from Hezron. They probably dwelt on the southern frontier of the tribe of Judah (vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.29">1Sa 30:29</reference>). The Kenites were protégés of Judah (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.6">1Sa 15:6</reference>, and Jdg 1:16). In <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.11">1Sa 27:11</reference> the writer introduces the remark, that in his raid David left neither man nor woman of his enemies alive, to take them to Gath, because he thought “they might report against us, and say, Thus hath David done.” There ought to be a major point under דּוד עשׂה, as the following clause does not contain the words of the slaughtered enemies, but is a clause appended by the historian himself, to the effect that David continued to act in that manner as long as he dwelt in the land of the Philistines. משׁפּט, the mode of procedure; lit. the right which he exercised (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.8.9">1Sa 8:9</reference>). <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.12">1Sa 27:12</reference> is connected with <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.10">1Sa 27:10</reference>; Achish believed David’s words, and said (to himself), “<hi type="italic">He hath made himself stinking</hi> (i.e., hated) <hi type="italic">among his own people, among Israel, and will be my servant</hi> (i.e., subject to me) <hi type="italic">for ever</hi>.” David in the Army of the Philistines. Attack upon Israel. Saul and the Witch of Endor - 1 Samuel 28 <div eID="gen4148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4149" type="x-p"/> The danger into which David had plunged through his flight into the land of the Philistines, and still more through the artifice with which he had deceived the king Achish as to his real feelings, was to be very soon made apparent to him. For example, when the Philistines went to war again with Israel, Achish summoned him to go with his men in the army of the Philistines to the war against his own people and land, and David could not disregard the summons. But even if he had not brought himself into this danger without some fault of his own, he had at any rate only taken refuge with the Philistines in the greatest extremity; and what further he had done, was only done to save his own life. The faithful covenant God helped him therefore out of this trouble, and very soon afterwards put an end to his persecution by the fact that Saul lost his life in the war.  <chapter eID="1Sam.27"/> <div eID="gen4149" type="x-p"/>

                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:243" />11 And David saved neither man nor woman alive, to bring <ns0:hi>tidings</ns0:hi> to Gath, saying, Lest they should tell on us <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">That the tidings of this Action against this People (who were, it seems, either tributaries to, or confederates with <ns0:hi>A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chish</ns0:hi>) might neither come quickly nor certainly to <ns0:hi>Achish</ns0:hi> his Court: which he might the rather promise himself, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause <ns0:hi>Achish</ns0:hi> and all his Men were now busily imployed in their Warlike preparations against the <ns0:hi>Israelites;</ns0:hi> and if any flying rumour came thither, he thought by his Interest and Artifices he could easily discredit and dash it. Besides the consideration of Gods Curse denounced against the People whom he had now destroyed, and of Gods particular Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mises made to him, and of his special Providence which he constantly experienced watching over him, made him more secure and confident in this and in many other hazardous attempts.</ns0:note>, saying, So did David, and so <ns0:hi>will be</ns0:hi> his manner all the while he dwelleth in the countrey of the Philistines.</ns0:p>
